cards.a: Latency, throughput, jitter, and loss, tying them to the network path. Tools include ping, traceroute, NetFlow, IP SLA, and protocol analyzers.

cards.q: What are the key performance metrics and their meanings?
cards.a: Latency (RTT delay), throughput (bits/sec), jitter (delay variation), loss (dropped percentage), and utilization (capacity use).

cards.q: What are the four components of latency?
cards.a: Serialization (link speed), propagation (distance), processing (router), and queueing (congestion). Latency equals all four combined.

cards.q: Why is jitter different from latency?
cards.a: Jitter is the variation in delay, not the level of delay itself.

cards.q: What tool measures jitter and loss, and what measures flows?
cards.a: IP SLA measures jitter/loss; NetFlow measures throughput and applications/flows.

cards.q: What does a constant high latency pattern indicate?
cards.a: Serialization delay or propagation distance, as opposed to spiking latency which indicates queueing.

cards.q: How is throughput different from bandwidth?
cards.a: Bandwidth is capacity, while throughput is what is actually delivered. TCP behavior often caps throughput before the link does.
The TCP window limits throughput, window scaling helps raise it, and drops shrink the window.

cards.q: What is the performance analysis workflow?
cards.a: Establish a baseline, measure latency/loss, identify the segment, capture traffic, then confirm the fix. Baseline, measure, isolate, capture, verify.

cards.q: What command shows the IP SLA measurement results?
What does traceroute reveal about performance when RTT is high?
cards.a: It pinpoints which hop is adding latency, helping isolate the failing segment.
